new.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
new.w: Current is measured in amperes (amps, A).
sol: 1 A means 1 coulomb of charge passes a point each second.
Volts measure push (voltage); ohms measure opposition (resistance).

new.q: What is the unit of resistance?
new.w: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).
sol: Resistance tells how hard it is to push current through a part.
1 Ω lets 1 A flow when 1 V pushes.

new.q: A toy motor runs on 6 V and draws 2 A. How many watts does it use?
new.w: Power is voltage times current.

new.q: A 4 Ω resistor carries 3 A. What voltage is across it?
new.w: Ohm's law: V = I × R.

new.q: Which wiring always gives an equivalent resistance LESS than any single resistor in it: series or parallel?
new.w: Parallel adds extra paths, so the total resistance falls below the smallest branch.
sol: More paths for current means less opposition overall.
Series adds resistance, so it ends up bigger than the largest.

new.q: Three bulbs are wired in SERIES to one battery. One filament breaks. What happens to the other two?
o: They go dark, because the loop is broken
They get dimmer but stay lit
new.w: A series circuit has only one path, so a break anywhere stops current everywhere.
sol: No path means zero current in every bulb.
Parallel bulbs would stay lit, because each has its own path.

new.q: Why must power be off before measuring a resistor with an ohmmeter?
o: The meter sends its own small current, and outside voltage would spoil the reading
The resistor changes value when powered
new.w: An ohmmeter finds resistance by pushing its own small current and seeing how much flows.
sol: Another source in the circuit adds extra current the meter cannot tell apart.
Also isolate the part so other paths do not read in parallel.

new.q: Two identical 9 V batteries are joined in PARALLEL (+ to +, − to −). The combined voltage is:
new.w: Parallel cells keep the same voltage but can supply more current for longer.
sol: Parallel cells share the load instead.
So voltage stays 9 V while capacity goes up.

new.q: Three 12 Ω resistors are in series. What is the total resistance in ohms?
new.w: Series resistances add.
sol: Same single path, so the opposition stacks up.

new.q: A 12 V source drives a 4 kΩ and a 2 kΩ resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 2 kΩ resistor?
new.w: Voltage divider: the 2 kΩ gets 2/6 of the 12 V.
sol: Share of voltage = share of resistance = 2/6 = 1/3.

new.q: A 60 W bulb runs for 5 minutes. How many joules does it use?
new.w: Energy = power × time, with time in seconds.

new.q: A 3000 mAh battery pack powers a robot that draws a steady 250 mA. About how many hours does it run?
new.w: Hours = capacity ÷ current.
sol: mAh means milliamp-hours: current times time.

new.q: A heater plugged into 120 V draws 10 A. What is its resistance in ohms?
new.w: Rearrange Ohm's law: R = V/I.

new.q: A resistor has 5 V across it and dissipates 0.5 W. What is its resistance in ohms?
new.w: Use P = V²/R, so R = V²/P.
sol: Check: I = P/V = 0.1 A, and 5 V ÷ 0.1 A = 50 Ω.

new.q: What single resistor, added in PARALLEL with a 100 Ω resistor, makes the pair equal 80 Ω? Give ohms.
new.w: Subtract conductances: 1/R = 1/80 − 1/100.
sol: Check: 100 × 400 ÷ 500 = 80 Ω. Adding a parallel part always lowers the total.

new.q: A 1.2 kW heater runs 3 hours. Electricity costs $0.30 per kWh. What is the cost in dollars?
new.w: Energy in kWh = kW × hours; cost = energy × price.

new.q: You need exactly 5 V across a 10 kΩ load from a 12 V supply, using one resistor in series with the load. What series resistance (in ohms) is needed?
new.w: The series resistor must drop the extra 7 V at the load's current.

new.q: Doubling the voltage across a fixed resistor makes its power how many times larger?
new.w: P = V²/R, so power grows with the square of the voltage.
sol: R stays the same, so current also doubles.

new.q: On a graph of voltage (vertical) against current (horizontal) for a resistor, the slope equals:
new.w: V = IR is a straight line through the origin, and its slope is R.
sol: Slope is rise over run, which is V/I.
A steeper line means a larger resistor.

new.q: Bulbs A and B are in parallel on an ideal battery. A switch is in series with B only. Closing the switch makes A:
o: unchanged, and the battery current rises
dimmer, and the battery current falls
brighter, and the battery current rises
unchanged, and the battery current stays the same
new.w: A still has the full battery voltage. The new branch adds current drawn from the battery.
sol: Each parallel branch sees the battery voltage by itself.
Total current = I_A + I_B goes up.

new.q: Four equal resistors are in series on 12 V. A voltmeter reads 0 V across R1, 0 V across R2, 12 V across R3 and 0 V across R4. The fault is:
new.w: With no current, only an open part can show the full source voltage.
sol: An open part has the whole voltage across its gap.
Others carry no current, so they have no drop.
A shorted R3 would read 0 V and the others would share 12 V.

new.q: A multimeter is set to measure current. To read the current through one resistor you must:
o: break the loop and insert the meter in series
place the leads across the resistor
touch the leads to the battery terminals
remove the resistor and leave a gap
new.w: The meter must carry the same current it measures.
sol: An ammeter has very low resistance.
Across a part it would act like a short and may blow its fuse.
So open the loop and put it in line.

new.q: Match each meter to how it is connected and its resistance.
pairs: Across a part with the power off
new.w: Each meter must not change the circuit it measures.
sol: A voltmeter must draw almost no current, so its resistance is huge.
An ammeter must add almost no resistance, so it is tiny.
An ohmmeter supplies its own current, so the circuit must be off.

new.q: Which is the correct power formula to use for two bulbs in PARALLEL when you know both resistances?
o: P = V²/R, because both have the same voltage
P = I²R, because both have the same current
P = V/R, because power is current
new.w: Parallel parts share voltage, so compare V²/R. Series parts share current, so compare I²R.
sol: Smaller R gives larger V²/R, so the smaller R is brighter.

new.q: One bulb lights on a battery. Then two such identical bulbs in SERIES are used on the same ideal battery. Each series bulb has what fraction of the single bulb's power?
new.w: Each bulb gets half the voltage and half the current, so one quarter the power.
sol: Series: total R doubles, so the current halves.
Each bulb now has half the voltage as well.

new.q: A wire's length and its diameter are both doubled. Its resistance becomes:
new.w: R grows with length but falls with cross-section area, and area goes as diameter squared.

new.q: A 120 V, 60 W bulb and a 120 V, 100 W bulb are wired in series across 120 V. Find the power in the 60 W bulb in watts.
new.w: Find each resistance from R = V²/P, then the series current.
sol: P = I²R = 0.3125² × 240 = 23.4 W. The 60 W bulb is brighter in series, because the larger resistance gets more power.

new.q: A 120 V circuit has a 15 A breaker. A 1500 W heater and a 600 W toaster are both plugged in (parallel). What total current do they draw?
new.w: Powers add; I = P/V.
sol: That is over 15 A, so the breaker trips.

new.q: Three 100 Ω, ¼ W resistors are in SERIES. What is the largest voltage across the whole string without exceeding any rating? Give volts.
new.w: Each resistor can carry I = √(P/R) = 0.05 A.

new.q: A 100 Ω and a 400 Ω resistor, each rated ¼ W, are in PARALLEL. What is the largest total power the pair can dissipate without exceeding a rating? Give watts.
new.w: Parallel means same voltage. The 100 Ω resistor reaches its limit first at 5 V.
sol: 400 Ω could take 10 V, so 5 V rules.

new.q: A 12 V source feeds node A. From A, 100 Ω goes to P and 300 Ω goes to Q. From P, 200 Ω goes to ground; from Q, 100 Ω goes to ground. A 100 Ω resistor links P to Q. Find the current in the link, in amps (magnitude).
new.w: Write KCL at P and at Q to find the two node voltages, then use Ohm's law on the link.

new.q: A balanced bridge: R1 = 120 Ω and R2 = 180 Ω form one side; R3 = 250 Ω and an unknown Rx form the other. The meter between the midpoints reads zero. Find Rx in ohms.
new.w: Zero meter current means both dividers have the same ratio: R1/R2 = R3/Rx.
sol: Same midpoint voltage means same ratio.

new.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the resistor joining the two midpoints carries:
o: no current, so removing it changes nothing
the same current as the source
new.w: Both midpoints sit at the same voltage, so nothing pushes current through the link.
sol: Balanced dividers give equal midpoint voltages.
No voltage difference means no current.
So you can take the link out or short it with no change.

new.q: A 12 V battery has internal resistance 0.5 Ω and powers a 5.5 Ω lamp. A second identical 5.5 Ω lamp is added in PARALLEL. What is the battery's terminal voltage afterward? Give volts.
new.w: More current means a bigger voltage drop inside the battery.
sol: Terminal V = 12 − 3.69 × 0.5 = 10.15 V, down from 11 V with one lamp.

new.q: A divider has two 10 kΩ resistors across 10 V. A voltmeter with 10 kΩ input resistance is placed across the lower resistor. What does it read? Give volts.
new.w: The meter is in parallel with the lower resistor and loads it.
sol: Not the 5 V you would expect: a real meter changes what it measures.

new.q: An ammeter of 2 Ω resistance is inserted in series in a circuit of 10 V and 8 Ω. What current does it read? Give amps.
new.w: The meter adds its own resistance to the loop.
sol: True current without the meter: 10/8 = 1.25 A.

new.q: A 12 V source has internal resistance 6 Ω. Compare the power delivered to a 3 Ω load and to a 12 Ω load.
o: The 12 Ω load gets twice as much
new.w: Two loads R1 and R2 give the same power when R1 × R2 = r². Here 3 × 12 = 6².
sol: Maximum power would come at 6 Ω, between the two.

new.q: A source has internal resistance 3 Ω and EMF 6 V. What is the maximum power it can deliver to any load? Give watts.
new.w: Maximum power transfer happens when R_load = r.
sol: P = I²R = 1 × 3 = 3 W. The other 3 W heats the source itself.

new.q: A 12 V battery drives a 1 kΩ and a 3 kΩ resistor in series, with the 1 kΩ next to the battery's + terminal. Ground is the node BETWEEN the resistors. What is the voltage of the battery's negative terminal?
new.w: Current is 3 mA. The 1 kΩ drops 3 V and the 3 kΩ drops 9 V. The negative terminal is 9 V below ground.
sol: Drops: 3 V across 1 kΩ, 9 V across 3 kΩ.
Ground is the middle node, so the + side is at +3 V and the − side is at −9 V.

new.q: Two 6 Ω resistors in series form a pair. That pair is in parallel with 3 Ω, and the combination is in series with 4 Ω. Find the total resistance in ohms.
new.w: Reduce from the inside out.

new.q: Rank these by power dissipated, largest first: 10 Ω across 12 V; 20 Ω across 12 V; 10 Ω and 20 Ω in series across 12 V; 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel across 12 V.
items: 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel across 12 V
10 Ω and 20 Ω in series across 12 V
new.w: P = V²/R_eq, so smaller equivalent resistance means more power at the same voltage.
sol: 10 Ω gives 14.4 W; 20 Ω gives 7.2 W.

new.q: A lamp is shining normally on an ideal battery. Select ALL changes that would make it dimmer.
o: Add a resistor in series with the lamp
Swap the battery for a lower-voltage one
Add a second lamp in series
Add a second lamp in parallel with the first
new.w: Dimmer means less current through the lamp. A parallel branch leaves the first lamp's voltage unchanged.
sol: A second lamp in series adds resistance.
An ideal battery keeps its voltage, so a parallel lamp changes nothing for the first.

new.q: Bulb A is in series with a parallel pair B and C (all identical, ideal battery). Bulb C burns out (open). What happens to A and B?
o: A gets dimmer and B gets brighter
A and B both get brighter
A gets brighter and B gets dimmer
A and B stay the same
new.w: Losing C leaves one path through B, so total resistance rises and current falls. B now carries all of it.
sol: Before: A carries I; B and C carry I/2 each.
After: total R rises (1.5 R to 2 R), so the current falls.
A has less current, so it dims. B now carries the full smaller current, which is bigger than before (I/2), so it brightens.

new.q: Two identical bulbs are in series on a battery. A wire is connected across bulb 1 only. Bulb 2 becomes:
new.w: The wire shorts bulb 1, so bulb 2 alone sets the current and gets the full voltage.
sol: Bulb 1 has about 0 V across it, so it goes out.
Total resistance halves, so current doubles.
Bulb 2 has twice the voltage and twice the current, so it is brighter.

new.q: A 6 V battery powers a 12 Ω, 24 Ω and 8 Ω resistor in parallel. How many watts does the battery supply in total?
new.w: In parallel each resistor has 6 V, and the powers add.
sol: The source supplies the sum: 3 + 1.5 + 4.5 = 9 W.

new.q: A 9 V battery feeds a 6 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find the power dissipated in the 3 Ω resistor in watts.
new.w: Find the pair's voltage first, then P = V²/R.
sol: I = 9/8 A, so the pair has 9/8 × 2 = 2.25 V.

new.q: Three parallel branches carry 2 A, 3 A and an unknown current. The source supplies 8 A, and the voltage across every branch is 4 V. What is the unknown branch's resistance in ohms?
new.w: KCL gives the missing branch current; then R = V/I.

new.q: A student wants to find a resistor's value from a voltmeter reading and an ammeter reading, and places the voltmeter across the resistor and ammeter together. What error is built in?
o: The voltmeter reads the resistor plus ammeter voltage, so R reads a little high
The ammeter reads the resistor current plus the voltmeter current, so R reads low
new.w: The voltmeter spans both the resistor and the ammeter's tiny resistance, so the voltage is slightly too big.
sol: Ammeter is in series with the resistor and carries the true current.
Voltmeter reads V across resistor + ammeter.
R_measured = (V_R + V_A)/I, a bit larger than R.

new.q: A 24 V source feeds two identical resistors in series. One resistor is then replaced by a wire (shorted), and the current rises from 2 A to what value in amps?
new.w: Shorting one of two equal series resistors halves the total resistance.
sol: Before: R_total = 24/2 = 12 Ω, so each is 6 Ω.

new.q: Kirchhoff's current law rests on the conservation of which quantity?
new.w: Charge cannot pile up at a node, so what flows in must flow out.
sol: Current is charge per second, so equal current means equal charge.

new.q: Wire A brings 4 A into a junction. Wire B takes 1.5 A out. Wire C is the only other wire. How many amps leave through C?
new.w: In = out: 4 = 1.5 + I.
sol: Charge in per second = charge out per second.

new.q: KVL says voltage changes around a closed loop add to zero. This follows from conservation of:
new.w: A charge that returns to its start has the same potential energy, so gains equal losses.
sol: Net change after a full loop = 0.

new.q: You trace a KVL loop through a resistor in the SAME direction as the current. The voltage change is:
new.w: Conventional current runs from higher to lower potential through a resistor.
sol: Against the current it would be +IR.

new.q: You guess a current's direction and your solution gives −2 A. This means:
o: the current really flows the other way, 2 A
the current is 2 A in your direction
new.w: A negative sign only says the true direction is opposite to your arrow.
sol: The size, 2 A, is still right.
Just reverse the arrow to fix the picture.

new.q: A node has three wires. 2 A flows in on one and 3 A flows in on another. The third wire carries:
new.w: All the charge arriving must leave: 2 + 3 = 5 A.
sol: Nothing can build up at a node.

new.q: A 14.4 V car alternator charges a 12 V battery (opposing) through 0.6 Ω in total. What is the charging current? Give amps.
new.w: The net EMF drives current through the resistance.

new.q: A jump-start joins a 12.6 V battery (0.02 Ω) to a dead 11 V battery (0.05 Ω) with cables of negligible resistance, + to + and − to −. What current flows in the loop? Give amps.
new.w: One loop: net EMF divided by total resistance.

new.q: Which is a correct KVL equation for one loop: a 10 V battery, 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series, clockwise current I?
new.w: The battery is a rise (+10). Each resistor is a drop (−IR). The sum is zero.
sol: Sum around the loop = 0, so I = 2 A.

new.q: Select ALL valid statements about KCL and KVL.
o: KCL applies at any node, even with batteries on the wires
KVL applies to any closed loop, even one with no battery
Counting current in as + and out as −, the sum at a node is zero
KVL says the current is the same everywhere in a loop
new.w: KCL is about nodes and KVL is about loops. Neither says currents are equal everywhere.
sol: KVL holds around every closed loop.
Equal current is only true for a series path, not a law.

new.q: Match each law to what it says.
pairs: Currents in = currents out at a node
Voltage changes around a loop sum to zero
new.w: Each law ties to a conservation idea or a component rule.
sol: Ohm's law relates one resistor's V and I.

new.q: Put the steps of the two-loop recipe in order.
items: Label a current and direction in each branch
Write KVL around two independent loops
Check power supplied equals power dissipated
new.w: Set up unknowns, write independent equations, solve, then verify.
sol: Arrows first (wrong guesses just give negative answers).
Solve, then check with power balance.

new.q: Node X has four wires: 3 A in, 5 A in, 2 A out, and an unknown wire carrying current OUT. How many amps is the unknown?
new.w: In = out: 3 + 5 = 2 + I.

new.q: A 12 V source is across a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find the current in the 3 Ω resistor of the pair. Give amps.
new.w: Reduce, find the total current, then use the voltage across the pair.
sol: I = 12/5 = 2.4 A; voltage across the pair = 2.4 × 2 = 4.8 V.

new.q: A 20 V battery drives two resistors in series. One drops 7.5 V. What does the other drop? Give volts.
new.w: KVL: the drops add up to the source voltage.

new.q: At a node, 4 A enters on wire 1 and 6 A enters on wire 2. Wire 3 carries 3 A out. How much must wire 4 carry?
new.w: In = out. Total in is 10 A; wire 3 takes 3 A, so wire 4 takes the other 7 A out.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 18 V with 3 Ω. Right branch: 12 V with 2 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the voltage across the shared resistor.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 3 A, I₂ = 1.5 A, I₃ = 4.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 9 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 28 V with 2 Ω. Right branch: 15 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the current in the left battery.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 6.75 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 7.25 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 14.5 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 12 V with 1 Ω. Right branch: 12 V with 4 Ω. Shared resistor: 4 Ω. Find the current in the shared resistor.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 2 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 10 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 21 V with 4 Ω. Right branch: 16 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 6 Ω. Find the power dissipated in the shared resistor.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 1.5 A, I₂ = 1 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 15 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 23 V with 2 Ω. Right branch: 20 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 4 Ω. Find the current in the right battery.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 2.5 A, I₂ = 2 A, I₃ = 4.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 18 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 21 V with 4 Ω. Right branch: 27 V with 2 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the current in the left battery.
new.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: Solving: I₁ = 1.5 A, I₂ = 6 A, I₃ = 7.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 15 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.

new.q: A 12 V battery (1 Ω) and a 6 V battery (1 Ω) are in parallel (+ to +) across a 2 Ω load. Find the current in the 6 V battery, magnitude in amps. (It may be charging.)
new.w: Find the common node voltage first, then each battery's current.
sol: Current out of the 6 V cell = (6 − 7.2)/1 = -1.2 A.
Negative means current flows INTO the 6 V battery: the stronger battery is charging it.

new.q: Two voltage dividers sit across the same 12 V. Point P: 100 Ω above and 200 Ω below. Point Q: 300 Ω above and 100 Ω below. No wire joins P and Q. Find V_P − V_Q in volts.
new.w: With no link, each divider is separate, so no loading.
sol: V_P − V_Q = 5 V. This is how a bridge detects an imbalance.

new.q: Three branches join at a top node and return to a common bottom node. Branch 1: 10 V source with 2 Ω. Branch 2: 4 V source with 1 Ω. Branch 3: just 4 Ω. Find the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor in volts.
new.w: KCL at the top node: the two source branches deliver current, and the 4 Ω takes it.

new.q: A circuit has 6 branches and 4 nodes. How many INDEPENDENT KVL loop equations are needed (using KCL at 3 of the nodes)?
new.w: Independent loops = branches − nodes + 1.
sol: Unknown currents = 6, so 6 equations are needed in all.

new.q: In a network, the sources supply 40 W but the resistors dissipate 45 W. What should you conclude?
o: There is an error: power must balance
This is normal for parallel branches
new.w: Energy is conserved, so supplied power equals dissipated power.
sol: A mismatch means a mistake in signs or arithmetic.
Use the check to catch errors.

new.q: Two batteries: E₁ = 10 V (1 Ω) and E₂ = 4 V (2 Ω) are in parallel with a 2 Ω load. How much power does the 10 V source supply (E₁ × I₁)? Give watts.
new.w: Find I₁ from the node voltage.

new.q: Going from A to B along the top path you meet a 6 V rise then a 2 V drop. The bottom path has one element. By KVL, how many volts does the bottom element change the potential from A to B? (rise positive)
new.w: The potential difference between two points is the same along every path.
sol: The bottom path must also give +4 V.
So the bottom element is a 4 V rise.

new.q: A loop has a 12 V battery and resistors R1 and R2 in series. A student writes 12 − IR1 + IR2 = 0. The error is:
o: IR2 should be a drop (−IR2), since the same current flows through it the same way
KVL should sum to the battery voltage, not zero
new.w: Both resistors are drops going with the current: 12 − IR1 − IR2 = 0.
sol: Same current direction through both resistors.
A sign flip on one resistor is the classic KVL mistake.

new.q: Four wires meet at a junction: A brings in 3 A, B takes out 8 A, C brings in 2 A. Wire D carries current INTO the junction. How many amps?
new.w: In = out: 3 + 2 + I_D = 8.

new.q: A 12 V battery (2 Ω) and a 3 V battery (1 Ω) are joined with OPPOSITE polarity across a shared 3 Ω resistor: the 3 V battery acts as −3 V at the top node. Find the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor in volts.
new.w: Treat the reversed battery as a −3 V source and write one node equation.

new.q: Two batteries E₁ = 12 V (R₁ = 2 Ω) and E₂ = 6 V (R₂ = 1 Ω) feed a shared 3 Ω resistor. Find the total power dissipated in all three resistors, in watts.
new.w: Find the three currents, then add I²R, or use power supplied = E₁I₁ + E₂I₂.
sol: Supplied = 12 × 2.73 + 6 × -0.545 = 29.5 W, and I²R adds to 29.5 W.

new.q: A network has 5 nodes. How many independent KCL equations can you write?
new.w: The last node's equation is just the sum of the others, so it adds nothing.
sol: Each node gives one KCL equation.
Add all five: every current appears once as in and once as out, giving 0 = 0.

new.q: A single loop has a 9 V source, a 3 Ω resistor and an unknown resistor R. The 3 Ω has 6 V across it. What is R?
new.w: KVL gives R's drop (3 V), and the loop current comes from the known resistor.

new.q: Currents of 2.4 A and 0.9 A flow into a node, and 1.5 A flows out on a third wire. The fourth wire carries:
new.w: Count everything in and everything out, then the leftover decides the direction.
sol: Still 1.8 A must leave, so wire four carries 1.8 A out.

report: Circuit Lab C4 (circ, kirch). Fixed 8 (unit bugs: circ-009 and circ-040 answers were in ohms but unit kΩ; circ-020 made unambiguous by adding internal resistance; kirch-011 ugly float; relevels). Deleted circ-296 (lemon cell voltage unverifiable and electrode-dependent) and kirch-012 (duplicate of kirch-002). Deleted 4 families: the 'current across kΩ resistor' family (answers in mA were given as e.g. 0.003 with unit mA, a x1000 error), and three trivial near-duplicates of the kcl/kvl/series-sum families (circ junction, circ three-series KVL, circ three-series sum). Added the new questions listed (~half level 3), all computed in python (c4_build.py). Remaining doubts: families not fully visible (only 3 variants shown) may hide other unit errors; the two-source 'shared branch' templates in kirch are all numerically alike.
